children.text: A software developer who likes writing about how to make things on the web, and why some small decisions turn out to matter most.
A place to write about software, design, and the thoughts that stop by now and then. No publishing schedule, and no newsletter funnel. Only the things I want to write down.
About this site
This site is built with Astro and EmDash, with an interface from HeroUI. Every post and page, including this one, can be edited from the admin.

data.title: Building for the Long Term
data.excerpt: Frameworks will change, and databases will change. What lasts is the clarity of how you think.

$media.alt: Code on a monitor in a dark room

children.text: Every few years this industry decides, all at once, that the way we have been working is wrong and that there is a better way. A new framework, a new paradigm, a new build tool. The cycle never stops, and if you are not careful you spend more time migrating than building.
I have been writing software long enough to watch several of those cycles. Each transition felt urgent at the time. Looking back, what actually mattered was rarely the framework.
What lasts
A clean data model lasts. Clear boundaries between systems last. Good names last. The choice to stay simple when something could have been made complicated — that lasts too.
Data structures that reflect the domain, not the taste of a framework.
Code someone else can read without asking the person who wrote it.
A short note on why a decision was made.
What does not last
What does not last is code written to impress, abstractions for problems that never arrive, and architecture that follows a framework's opinion instead of the domain.
The best code I have written is boring. It reads like prose and does one thing well.
The worst code I have written felt very clever at the time. I remember that lesson whenever I am tempted to build something smart.

data.title: Why Choose a Static Site
data.excerpt: A static site is not a step backward. It is what you get when you take performance and simplicity seriously.

$media.alt: A laptop and a cup of coffee on a wooden desk

children.text: There is a small irony in the history of the web: it started static, became dynamic, and is slowly returning to static. A static site today is not a hand-typed HTML page from 1998. It is generated, optimized, and served from an edge network in milliseconds.

The promise of server-side rendering for everything is appealing: dynamic content, personalization, real-time data. Most sites do not need all of that almost all of the time. A blog post does not need to be rendered again on every request.
The performance argument

A static file served from a CDN is the fastest thing the web can hand you. No cold start, no database query, no rendering work on a server. The first response time is basically the network latency to the nearest edge.
Just enough interactivity
When dynamic behavior is actually needed, add it precisely. An interactive island in a sea of static HTML. You get the best of both, without paying for both on every request.

data.title: Small Tools, Large Impact
data.excerpt: The best developer tools do one thing well and then get out of your way.

$media.alt: Wrenches and hand tools hanging on a workshop wall

children.text: There is a class of software that rarely gets praised. Not frameworks, platforms, or IDEs, but small sharp tools that solve one problem so well you forget you are using them. Becoming invisible is the highest praise a tool can get.

Ripgrep, for example, searches code so fast it changed how I think about search. Or jq, which makes JSON feel like a first-class data format in the terminal. Or curl, which has quietly held up the pipes of the internet for decades.
The Unix philosophy, revisited

Do one thing well. The advice is old enough to sound like a cliché, but the best modern tools still follow it. They do not try to become a platform. They do their job and can be composed with other tools.

The temptation to add is always there: one more feature, one more option, one more integration. Each addition is a decision someone has to make and a code path someone has to maintain. The best tools resist that temptation, and because they stay small, they stay reliable.

data.title: Designing with Constraints
data.excerpt: A constraint is not a barrier to creativity. A constraint is the structure that makes creativity possible.

$media.alt: Pencils and design tools on a desk

children.text: Give a designer a blank canvas and unlimited time, and the result is often ordinary. Give a tight brief, a small screen, and a deadline, and the result can surprise you. That is not a paradox. That is how creativity works.
Constraints force decisions. When you may use only two typefaces, you choose carefully. When a page has to load in under a second, every element has to earn its place.
Embracing the box

The web itself is a constraint. HTML flows in one direction. CSS has a box model. Browsers have viewport sizes and their own ideas about rendering type. You can fight those constraints or work with them, and the results are very different.
The design I admire most does not look forced through a framework. It looks like it grew out of its medium, following the grain instead of fighting it.
